extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent applicants (patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners on evaluating indefiniteness, means‑plus‑function limitations, written description, enablement, and patentability of computer‑implemented functional claim language during prosecution. Focuses on Office actions, interviews, claim interpretation, and record-keeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural support required for software-based means-plus-function limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A means-plus-function limitation that corresponds to software per se (i.e., only supported by software and not by an algorithm and the computer or microprocessor programmed with the algorithm) should be deemed indefinite and rejected under § 112, ¶ 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not construe the limitation as covering pure software implementation absent corresponding structure disclosed in the specification. A claim that includes such a limitation is not necessarily directed to software per se as a whole if other structural limitations exist, but the means-plus-function limitation itself requires corresponding structure (e.g., algorithm and programmed device) or it is indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must establish a clear record when asserting indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should carefully provide a complete and accurate picture of the Office’s consideration and must clearly explain all actions taken during prosecution, avoiding mere conclusions that a term is indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rejecting under § 112, ¶ 2, provide findings and reasons supporting the rejection. MPEP § 2173.05 gives examples of rationales (functional claim limitations, relative terminology, lack of antecedent basis, etc.). A clear record enhances prosecution clarity and benefits public notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action must set forth specific term and why metes and bounds are unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: An Office action rejecting under § 112, ¶ 2 must identify the specific term or phrase deemed indefinite and explain in detail why that term renders the metes and bounds of the claim unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient information for applicant to prepare a meaningful response (explain what is indefinite and why, and, where practicable, indicate how indefiniteness may be resolved). Claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation during prosecution to facilitate clarifying claims at the application stage. Quote: 'Because claims delineate the patentee’s right to exclude...' (to emphasize public notice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on statutory threshold clarity rather than stylistic improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: The examination focus under § 112, ¶ 2 is whether claim language meets the statutory threshold of clarity and precision, not whether the examiner prefers alternate wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If language satisfies § 112, ¶ 2 but could be made clearer, suggest improved claim language rather than issue an indefiniteness rejection. When more information is needed to ascertain meaning, consider a requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105 (see MPEP § 704.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice compact prosecution: identify all grounds and state claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the initial review and first Office action, examiners should review claims for compliance with all statutory requirements and identify all applicable grounds of rejection, stating how ambiguous claim terms are being interpreted when applying prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject each claim on all reasonable grounds (e.g., § 112 ¶ 2 and § 102/§ 103 based on examiner's interpretation) to avoid piecemeal examination. When rejecting over prior art, state on the record how the claim term or phrase is being interpreted with respect to the applied art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt interview when indefiniteness is sole issue; make interview record explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: If indefiniteness is the only outstanding issue, examiners should attempt to resolve it through an interview before issuing a rejection, and the substance of any interview must be made of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews can clarify broadest reasonable interpretation, meaning of claim limitations, scope of preamble language, functional language, intended use language, and means-plus-function limitations. Record examples: why term is/is not sufficiently clear, consistency with specification, why § 112, ¶ 6 is/ is not invoked and identification of corresponding structure, any claim amendments discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide claim interpretation in reasons for allowance when record is unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: When the prosecution record does not make clear the examiner’s reasons for allowing a claim, the examiner may set forth such reasoning in reasons for allowance pursuant to 37 CFR 1.104(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons for allowance improve the quality and reliability of issued patents by clarifying why the claim is allowable (e.g., the claim interpretation applied relative to prior art). However, avoid placing unwarranted broad or narrow interpretations upon the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: When invoking § 112, ¶ 6, state the basis and identify corresponding structure
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation is interpreted as invoking § 112, ¶ 6 (means/step‑plus‑function), the Office action should state that the limitation is being treated under ¶ 6 and explain why, and identify the corresponding structure in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain when non‑'means for' language (e.g., 'module for') is treated under ¶ 6 (functional term coupled to non‑structural word). If corresponding structure is not clearly identifiable, still attempt to identify the structure most closely associated with the means-plus-function limitation to facilitate a prior art search. When allowing such a claim, indicate that ¶ 6 was applied and clarify the associated structure if not apparent in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement for computer-implemented functional claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy § 112, ¶ 1 written description, the specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude the inventor possessed the claimed invention, including for computer‑implemented functional claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic claim language or claiming in purely functional terms without describing species that achieve the function may fail written description (Ariad, LizardTech). For computer‑implemented inventions, determine whether the specification discloses the computer and the algorithm (necessary steps/flowcharts) that perform the claimed function in sufficient detail such that one skilled in the art could program the disclosed computer to perform the claimed function (e.g., Hayes example where algorithmic steps were described). If not, make a § 112, ¶ 1 written description rejection. See MPEP §§ 2161.01–2163.07(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement for computer-implemented functional claims (undue experimentation/Wands factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must enable the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation; assess enablement using the Wands factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the Wands factors: (1) breadth of the claims; (2) nature of the invention; (3) state of the prior art; (4) level of skill in the art; (5) predictability in the art; (6) amount of direction provided by the inventor; (7) existence of working examples; (8) quantity of experimentation needed. Functional claim language that is broad because it is not limited to particular structure may raise enablement concerns — the claim scope must be commensurate with the disclosure. Examples: Sitrick (spec enabled video games but not movies); Auto. Techs. (failure to disclose how to make an electronic side impact sensor). See MPEP §§ 2161.01, 2164.01(a)–2164.08(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability considerations for computer-implemented functional claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional claim language that covers all devices capable of performing a recited function may be anticipated or obvious if the prior art inherently or predictably performs that function, and the term 'computer' should be given its broadest reasonable meaning consistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior art discloses a device capable of inherently performing the claimed function, a § 102 or § 103 rejection may be appropriate. A claim using 'computer' is not limited to a particular kind of computer unless modified or defined in the specification (In re Paulsen). Implementing a known function on a general‑purpose computer may be obvious if it is a predictable use of prior art elements; adapting existing processes to Internet/browser tech has been found obvious. See MPEP §§ 2112, 2114 and KSR-related guidance (Examination Guidelines Update).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function (¶6) applies only to purely functional limitations lacking structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Means-plus-function claiming applies only to purely functional limitations that do not provide the structure that performs the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Phillips, determine whether claim language provides structural meaning; if it does not, treat under § 112, ¶ 6 and require disclosure of corresponding structure in the specification. Refer to MPEP § 2173.05 and relevant case law when making this determination.
